definitions: affect: to change or influence | effect: a change caused by something
example: Lack of sleep can affect your memory. | Music has a calming effect on babies.
typical_mistake: It has a big affect on me.
correction: It has a big effect on me.
mistake_note: After a/the/big you need the noun effect.
memory_tip: Affect = Action (verb), Effect = End result (noun).

definitions: say: speak words | tell: give information to a person
example: She said that she was tired. | She told me the truth.
typical_mistake: He said me that…
correction: He told me that…
mistake_note: A listener right after the verb → tell.
memory_tip: tell + person; say + words (or say to sb). Fixed: tell a story/the truth/a lie, say sorry.

definitions: make: create or produce | do: perform an activity or task
example: Can you make a cake for the party? | I need to do my homework.
typical_mistake: I made my homework.
correction: I did my homework.
memory_tip: make = create (a decision, a mistake, money, progress); do = activities (homework, research, your best).

definitions: borrow: take and use, then return | lend: give for a short time
example: Can I borrow your charger? | Could you lend me ten dollars?
typical_mistake: Can you borrow me your pen?
correction: Can you lend me your pen?
mistake_note: You receive → borrow; you give → lend.
memory_tip: Borrow brings it to you (borrow from sb); lend sends it away (lend to sb).

definitions: lie: be in a flat position | lay: put something down
example: I'm going to lie down for a bit. | Please lay the papers on the desk.
typical_mistake: Yesterday I laid on the sofa all afternoon.
correction: Yesterday I lay on the sofa all afternoon.
mistake_note: No object → lie – lay – lain; laid is the past of lay (put down).
memory_tip: Trap: the past of lie is lay. lie (tell a lie) – lied – lied.

definitions: rise: go up by itself | raise: lift or increase something
example: The sun rises in the east. | The shop raised its prices.
typical_mistake: The price of petrol has raised a lot.
correction: The price of petrol has risen a lot.
memory_tip: Raise always takes an object (raise something); rise never does: prices rise, a shop raises prices.

definitions: bring: carry towards the speaker | take: carry away from the speaker
example: Please bring your laptop when you come here. | Don't forget to take an umbrella when you go out.
typical_mistake: I'll bring the kids to school before I go to work.
correction: I'll take the kids to school before I go to work.
mistake_note: Carrying away from where you are → take.
memory_tip: Bring = towards the speaker (here); take = away from the speaker (there).

definitions: see: notice with your eyes | look: turn your eyes on purpose | watch: look at something for a time
example: Did you see that lightning? | Look at this picture! | We watched the match on TV.
typical_mistake: I like seeing football on TV.
correction: I like watching football on TV.
mistake_note: Following something for a time → watch.
memory_tip: See just happens; look at is on purpose (often still things); watch is for a while, usually something moving (TV, a match).

definitions: hear: notice a sound | listen: pay attention to a sound
example: Can you hear that noise? | Listen to me carefully.
typical_mistake: I listen music every day.
correction: I listen to music every day.
memory_tip: Hear just happens; listen is on purpose. With an object it is always listen to.

definitions: speak: use a language; talk formally | talk: have a conversation
example: Do you speak Japanese? | We talked about our plans for hours.
typical_mistake: She can talk three languages.
correction: She can speak three languages.
memory_tip: Speak + a language (speak English) or formal speech; talk = have a conversation (talk to/with sb, about sth).

definitions: learn: gain knowledge or a skill | study: spend time learning a subject
example: I learnt to swim last summer. | She is studying medicine at university.
typical_mistake: I studied to ride a bike when I was six.
correction: I learned to ride a bike when I was six.
mistake_note: Gaining a skill → learn to + verb.
memory_tip: Study is the effort (study for an exam); learn is the result – now you know it (learn to swim).

definitions: remember: keep in your memory | remind: make someone remember
example: I can't remember his name. | Please remind me to call Mum.
typical_mistake: Remember me to call her.
correction: Remind me to call her.
memory_tip: Remind needs another person: remind sb to do / of sth; remember happens in your own head.

definitions: rob: take from a person or place | steal: take a thing illegally
example: Two men robbed the bank. | Someone stole my bike.
typical_mistake: Someone robbed my phone on the bus.
correction: Someone stole my phone on the bus.
mistake_note: The object is a thing → steal.
memory_tip: You rob a person or place (rob a bank); you steal a thing (steal a bike from sb).

definitions: win: be first in a game | beat: defeat an opponent
example: Vietnam won the match. | Vietnam beat Thailand 2–0.
typical_mistake: We won them.
correction: We beat them.
mistake_note: win a game/prize; beat an opponent.
memory_tip: Win + a game, prize or medal; beat + the opponent.

definitions: fun: enjoyable | funny: making you laugh
example: The party was really fun. | He told a funny joke.
typical_mistake: The trip was funny – we enjoyed every minute.
correction: The trip was fun – we enjoyed every minute.
memory_tip: Fun = enjoyable (a fun day); funny = makes you laugh (a funny joke).

definitions: economic: related to the economy | economical: not wasting money or fuel
example: The country faces serious economic problems. | This car is very economical to run.
typical_mistake: This heater is very economic to run.
correction: This heater is very economical to run.
memory_tip: Economic = about the economy (economic growth); economical = saves money (an economical car).

definitions: historic: important in history | historical: related to the past
example: It was a historic victory. | She writes historical novels.
typical_mistake: I enjoy historic films about ancient China.
correction: I enjoy historical films about ancient China.
mistake_note: Set in the past (films, novels) → historical.
memory_tip: Historic = important in history (a historic day); historical = about the past (historical records).

definitions: classic: of high quality, typical | classical: traditional; of ancient Greece/Rome
example: Casablanca is a classic film. | I listen to classical music.
typical_mistake: She plays classic music on the piano.
correction: She plays classical music on the piano.
memory_tip: Classical = the classical tradition or ancient Greece/Rome (classical music); classic = a top, typical example (a classic film, a classic mistake).

definitions: sensible: showing good judgement | sensitive: easily upset or affected
example: That's a sensible decision. | She is very sensitive to criticism.
typical_mistake: My skin is very sensible to the sun.
correction: My skin is very sensitive to the sun.
memory_tip: Sensible = showing good sense (not 'sensitive'); sensitive = easily hurt or affected.

definitions: especially: above all; particularly | specially: for a particular purpose
example: I love fruit, especially mangoes. | This cake was made specially for you.
typical_mistake: I like sports, specially football.
correction: I like sports, especially football.
memory_tip: Especially = above all; specially = for one purpose (made specially for you).

definitions: beside: next to | besides: in addition (to)
example: Come and sit beside me. | Besides English, she speaks French.
typical_mistake: Beside, the hotel is close to the beach.
correction: Besides, the hotel is close to the beach.
mistake_note: 'In addition' at the start of a sentence → Besides.
memory_tip: Beside = next to; add an s for 'in addition' → besides.

definitions: between: in the middle of two | among: surrounded by a group
example: The park is between the bank and the school. | The singer is popular among teenagers.
typical_mistake: The house is among the river and the forest.
correction: The house is between the river and the forest.
memory_tip: Between = separate, clear items (often two); among = inside a group or crowd.

definitions: for: over a period of | since: from a point in time
example: I've lived here for ten years. | I've lived here since 2015.
typical_mistake: I have studied English since 5 years.
correction: I have studied English for 5 years.
memory_tip: For + a period (for three years); since + a starting point (since 2015, since Monday).

definitions: during: at some time in | for: how long
example: I fell asleep during the film. | I slept for two hours.
typical_mistake: I stayed in Da Nang during three days.
correction: I stayed in Da Nang for three days.
memory_tip: During + an event or period (when?); for + a length of time (how long?).

definitions: ago: before now | before: earlier than; at any time in the past
example: We met three years ago. | I had met her two years before the wedding.
typical_mistake: I met him three years before, at university.
correction: I met him three years ago, at university.
memory_tip: Ago counts back from now, with the past simple (two days ago); before counts back from another past time (two days before the trip).

definitions: already: before now | yet: until now
example: I've already finished. | I haven't finished yet.
typical_mistake: I haven't already finished.
correction: I haven't finished yet.
memory_tip: Already = sooner than expected, in positive sentences, mid-sentence; yet = in negatives and questions, usually at the end.

definitions: still: continuing | yet: until now (negative)
example: It's still raining. | It hasn't stopped yet.
typical_mistake: It's yet raining.
correction: It's still raining.
memory_tip: Still = something continues (before the main verb); yet in negatives = it hasn't happened (at the end).

definitions: every: all members of a group | each: every one, separately
example: Every student in the school wears a uniform. | She had a bag in each hand.
typical_mistake: She wore a ring on every hand.
correction: She wore a ring on each hand.
memory_tip: Each = one by one, separately (works for two); every = all as a group (three or more). Both take a singular noun.

definitions: a few: some, a small number | few: not many
example: I have a few friends here, so I'm not lonely. | Few people understood the lecture, so it was a failure.
typical_mistake: Don't worry, I have few friends here who can help.
correction: Don't worry, I have a few friends here who can help.
memory_tip: A few = some, enough (positive); few = almost none (negative). Both + plural countable nouns.

definitions: a little: some, a small amount | little: not much
example: There's a little milk left – enough for your tea. | There's little hope of finding them now.
typical_mistake: Hurry up! We have a little time left.
correction: Hurry up! We have little time left.
memory_tip: A little = some, enough (positive); little = almost none (negative). Both + uncountable nouns.

definitions: fewer: a smaller number of | less: a smaller amount of
example: There were fewer cars on the road. | You should eat less sugar.
typical_mistake: There were less people than last year.
correction: There were fewer people than last year.
memory_tip: Things you count (cars, people) → fewer; things you measure (sugar, time) → less.

definitions: many: a large number of | much: a large amount of
example: How many books do you have? | How much water do you drink?
typical_mistake: I don't have much friends.
correction: I don't have many friends.
memory_tip: Many + plural countable nouns; much + uncountable nouns. In positive sentences a lot of sounds more natural.

definitions: alone: without other people | lonely: sad because you are alone
example: She lives alone. | He feels lonely in the big city.
typical_mistake: I like living lonely.
correction: I like living alone.
memory_tip: Alone = without other people (a fact); lonely = sad about it (a feeling). You can be alone without being lonely.

definitions: bored: feeling no interest | boring: not interesting
example: I was bored during the lesson. | The lesson was boring.
typical_mistake: I'm boring in this class.
correction: I'm bored in this class.
memory_tip: General rule: -ed = how you feel; -ing = what causes the feeling.

definitions: interested: wanting to know more | interesting: catching your attention
example: I'm interested in history. | History is interesting.
typical_mistake: I am interesting in music.
correction: I am interested in music.
memory_tip: -ed = how you feel (interested in); -ing = what makes you feel it (an interesting book).

definitions: excited: very happy and eager | exciting: making you excited
example: The children are excited about Tet. | It was an exciting match.
typical_mistake: I'm so exciting about the trip.
correction: I'm so excited about the trip.
memory_tip: Excited = how a person feels (excited about); exciting = what causes it (an exciting trip).

definitions: job: a paid position | work: activity; the place you work
example: She got a new job at a bank. | I have a lot of work to do today.
typical_mistake: I'm looking for a work.
correction: I'm looking for a job. / I'm looking for work.
mistake_note: work is uncountable – no a work.
memory_tip: Job is countable (a job, two jobs); work is uncountable and general (a lot of work, go to work).

definitions: travel: going to places in general | trip: a short visit somewhere | journey: the act of travelling from one place to another
example: Air travel is getting cheaper. | We went on a day trip to Ha Long. | The journey from Hanoi to Hue takes 12 hours.
typical_mistake: I had a nice travel.
correction: I had a nice trip.
mistake_note: travel as a noun is usually uncountable.
memory_tip: Travel = travelling in general (usually uncountable); trip = a visit there and back (a business trip); journey = getting from A to B.

definitions: advice: an opinion about what to do | advise: tell someone what to do
example: Can you give me some advice? | I advise you to rest.
typical_mistake: She gave me many advices.
correction: She gave me a lot of advice.
memory_tip: Advice (with c, said /s/) is the noun; advise (with s, said /z/) is the verb.

definitions: practice: regular training | practise: do regularly to improve
example: Football practice is on Monday. | You need to practise every day.
typical_mistake: We have football practise on Monday.
correction: We have football practice on Monday.
mistake_note: The noun is always practice (UK and US).
memory_tip: American English uses practice for both.

definitions: principal: head of a school; main | principle: a basic rule or belief
example: The principal gave a speech. | It's against my principles.
typical_mistake: It's a matter of principal.
correction: It's a matter of principle.
memory_tip: The principal is your pal (head of a school; main); a principle is a rule (both end in -le).

definitions: compliment: an expression of praise | complement: something that goes well with
example: Thanks for the compliment! | The wine is a perfect complement to the meal.
typical_mistake: She complemented me on my English.
correction: She complimented me on my English.
memory_tip: Compliment = praise (I like it!); complement = makes something complete.

definitions: stationary: not moving | stationery: paper, pens, etc.
example: The traffic was stationary for an hour. | We sell stationery and books.
typical_mistake: I bought some stationary for school.
correction: I bought some stationery for school.
memory_tip: Stationary = standing still; stationery = envelopes, paper and pens.

definitions: lose: stop having; fail to win | loose: not tight
example: Don't lose your passport. | These jeans are too loose.
typical_mistake: I don't want to loose my job.
correction: I don't want to lose my job.
memory_tip: Lose /luːz/ is the verb and has lost an o; loose /luːs/ is the adjective, with room for two.

definitions: quiet: making little noise | quite: fairly
example: The library is very quiet. | The test was quite hard.
typical_mistake: Please be quite in the library.
correction: Please be quiet in the library.
memory_tip: Quiet /ˈkwaɪət/ has two syllables = silent; quite /kwaɪt/ has one = fairly.

definitions: than: used in comparisons | then: next; at that time
example: She is taller than me. | We had lunch and then went shopping.
typical_mistake: My sister is older then me.
correction: My sister is older than me.
memory_tip: Than is for comparing; then is for when and next.

definitions: its: belonging to it | it's: it is; it has
example: The dog wagged its tail. | It's raining again.
typical_mistake: The company changed it's name.
correction: The company changed its name.
memory_tip: Test: replace it with it is or it has. If that works, write it's; if not, write its (possessive, like his).

definitions: their: belonging to them | there: in that place | they're: they are
example: The students left their bags here. | There are three reasons. | They're coming tomorrow.
typical_mistake: Their are many problems.
correction: There are many problems.
memory_tip: Their contains heir (ownership); there contains here (place, there is); they're = they are.

definitions: whose: belonging to which person | who's: who is; who has
example: Whose phone is this? | Who's coming to the party?
typical_mistake: Who's bag is this?
correction: Whose bag is this?
memory_tip: Test: replace it with who is or who has. If that works, who's; if it means 'belonging to whom', whose.

definitions: your: belonging to you | you're: you are
example: Is this your coat? | You're welcome!
typical_mistake: Your welcome!
correction: You're welcome!
memory_tip: Test: replace it with you are. If that works, you're; if not, your (belonging to you).

definitions: accept: agree to take | except: not including
example: Please accept my apology. | Everyone came except Tom.
typical_mistake: I except your invitation.
correction: I accept your invitation.
memory_tip: Accept (verb) = take or agree to; except (preposition) = not including – ex- means 'out'.

definitions: adapt: change to fit | adopt: take as your own
example: Animals adapt to their environment. | The school adopted a new policy.
typical_mistake: It took me months to adopt to life in London.
correction: It took me months to adapt to life in London.
memory_tip: Adapt = change to fit (adapt to); adopt = take as your own (adopt a child, adopt a policy).

definitions: emigrate: leave your country to live elsewhere | immigrate: come into a country to live
example: His family emigrated from Vietnam in 1990. | Many people immigrate to Canada every year.
typical_mistake: His family immigrated from Vietnam in 1990.
correction: His family emigrated from Vietnam in 1990.
memory_tip: Emigrate = exit your country (from); immigrate = come in to a new one (to). Same move, different point of view.

definitions: prevent: stop something happening | avoid: keep away from
example: Vaccines prevent disease. | I avoid eating fried food.
typical_mistake: The rain avoided us from going out.
correction: The rain prevented us from going out.
memory_tip: Prevent = stop something happening (prevent sb from doing); avoid = keep yourself away (avoid + -ing).

definitions: fit: be the right size | suit: look good on; be convenient | match: go well together
example: These shoes don't fit me – they're too small. | Red really suits you. | Your bag matches your shoes.
typical_mistake: This dress doesn't suit me – it's too tight.
correction: This dress doesn't fit me – it's too tight.
memory_tip: Fit = the right size; suit = looks good on a person, or is convenient; match = two things go together.

definitions: expect: think something will happen | wait: stay until something happens | look forward to: feel happy about something coming
example: I expect it will rain later. | I'm waiting for the bus. | I'm looking forward to the holiday.
typical_mistake: I look forward to see you.
correction: I look forward to seeing you.
memory_tip: Expect = think it will happen; wait for = spend time until it happens; look forward to + -ing = feel happy about it.

definitions: hope: want something possible | wish: want something unreal
example: I hope you pass the exam. | I wish I were taller.
typical_mistake: I wish you will pass the exam.
correction: I hope you pass the exam.
memory_tip: Hope = something possible (hope + present/future); wish = something unreal (wish + past: I wish I were…).

definitions: opportunity: a good time to do something | possibility: something that might happen | chance: opportunity; likelihood
example: The job is a great opportunity to learn. | There is a possibility of rain. | Is there any chance you could help me?
typical_mistake: This job gives me the possibility to travel.
correction: This job gives me the opportunity to travel.
mistake_note: A chance to do something → opportunity to.
memory_tip: Opportunity = a good moment to do something (to do); possibility = something might happen (of); chance can mean both and is less formal.

definitions: price: the money asked for something | cost: money needed to do or get something
example: The shop cut its prices for the sale. | The cost of living in cities is high.
typical_mistake: The price of living in Hanoi is rising.
correction: The cost of living in Hanoi is rising.
mistake_note: Fixed phrase: the cost of living.
memory_tip: Price = what the seller asks; cost = what you must spend to do or get something (the cost of living).

definitions: salary: fixed yearly or monthly pay | wage: pay per hour or week
example: Teachers' salaries are paid monthly. | The minimum wage rose this year.
typical_mistake: The minimum salary rose this year.
correction: The minimum wage rose this year.
memory_tip: Salary = fixed monthly or yearly pay; wage = paid by the hour or week (the minimum wage).

definitions: house: a building to live in | home: the place where you live
example: They bought a big house by the sea. | I want to go home.
typical_mistake: I go to home after school.
correction: I go home after school.
mistake_note: No to before home after verbs of movement.
memory_tip: House = the building; home = where you live and belong. go/come/get home – no to.

definitions: ensure: make certain something happens | insure: buy insurance for | assure: tell someone confidently
example: Please ensure that all doors are locked. | You should insure your car. | I can assure you that it's safe.
typical_mistake: I ensure you that it's safe.
correction: I assure you that it's safe.
memory_tip: Ensure = make sure it happens; insure = buy insurance; assure = tell a person confidently (assure sb that…).

definitions: convince: make someone believe | persuade: make someone do
example: She convinced me that she was right. | He persuaded me to join.
typical_mistake: He convinced that me to join.
correction: He persuaded me to join.
memory_tip: convince sb to V is common now; convince sb that is the core use.

definitions: discover: find something that existed | invent: create something new
example: Fleming discovered penicillin. | Who invented the telephone?
typical_mistake: Who discovered the telephone?
correction: Who invented the telephone?
memory_tip: Discover = find something that already existed (a planet, a law of nature); invent = create something new (a machine).

words: at the end / in the end
definitions: at the end: at the final point of | in the end: finally, after a long time
example: Sign your name at the end of the form. | In the end, we decided to stay.
typical_mistake: In the end of the film, they get married.
correction: At the end of the film, they get married.
mistake_note: Followed by of → at the end of.
memory_tip: At the end of sth = the final point of it; in the end = finally, after everything (stands alone).

definitions: on time: at the planned time | in time: early enough
example: The train left on time. | We got to the cinema just in time to see the start.
typical_mistake: We arrived on time to catch the last bus.
correction: We arrived in time to catch the last bus.
mistake_note: Early enough to do something → in time to.
memory_tip: On time = at the planned time; in time = early enough (in time for sth / to do).

definitions: like: similar to | as: in the role of
example: She sings like an angel. | He works as a nurse.
typical_mistake: She works like a teacher.
correction: She works as a teacher.
mistake_note: A real job or role → as.
memory_tip: Like = similar to (not really); as = in the role of (really).

definitions: sometimes: on some occasions | sometime: at an unknown time
example: I sometimes cook dinner. | Let's meet sometime next week.
typical_mistake: Let's have dinner together sometimes next week.
correction: Let's have dinner together sometime next week.
memory_tip: With -s = several times → sometimes; without → sometime (at some point).

definitions: every day: each day | everyday: ordinary, daily
example: I exercise every day. | Smartphones are part of everyday life.
typical_mistake: I go jogging everyday.
correction: I go jogging every day.
memory_tip: Everyday (one word) is an adjective before a noun; every day = each day. If every single day works, write two words.

definitions: maybe: perhaps | may be: might be
example: Maybe we should leave. | The shop may be closed today.
typical_mistake: He maybe late today.
correction: He may be late today.
mistake_note: The sentence needs a verb → may be.
memory_tip: Maybe (one word) = perhaps, usually at the start; may be is a verb – if might be works, write two words.

definitions: farther: at a greater distance | further: additional; more
example: The station is farther than I thought. | For further information, call us.
typical_mistake: The beach is more far than I thought.
correction: The beach is farther than I thought.
memory_tip: Physical distance: farther or further; 'more, additional' is only further (further information). Never more far.

definitions: older: of greater age | elder: older (family, before a noun)
example: My brother is older than me. | My elder sister lives in Paris.
typical_mistake: My brother is two years elder than me.
correction: My brother is two years older than me.
memory_tip: Elder is for family members, before a noun (my elder sister); with than always use older.

definitions: continuous: without a break | continual: happening again and again
example: There was continuous rain for three days. | I'm tired of your continual complaints.
typical_mistake: We had continual rain for 48 hours without stopping.
correction: We had continuous rain for 48 hours without stopping.
memory_tip: Continuous = without a break (one unbroken line); continual = again and again, with breaks (often annoying).

definitions: effective: producing the result you want | efficient: working well without waste
example: This medicine is very effective. | An efficient engine uses less fuel.
typical_mistake: This engine is very effective – it uses little fuel.
correction: This engine is very efficient – it uses little fuel.
memory_tip: Effective = gets the result you want; efficient = does it without wasting time, money or energy.

definitions: imply: suggest without saying directly | infer: reach a conclusion
example: Are you implying that I'm lying? | From his tone, I inferred that he was angry.
typical_mistake: Are you inferring that I'm lying?
correction: Are you implying that I'm lying?
memory_tip: The speaker implies; the listener infers. Meaning goes out of the speaker and into the listener.

definitions: altogether: in total; completely | all together: everyone at once
example: That's 50 dollars altogether. | Let's sing all together now.
typical_mistake: That will be 30 dollars all together.
correction: That will be 30 dollars altogether.
memory_tip: Altogether = in total; completely; all together = everyone at once (you can split it: we all went together).

definitions: alive: not dead (after a verb) | live: living (before a noun); broadcast now
example: Is the fish still alive? | They sell live fish at the market.
typical_mistake: They sell alive crabs at the market.
correction: They sell live crabs at the market.
memory_tip: Alive goes after a verb (is alive); live /laɪv/ goes before a noun (live fish, live music).

definitions: damage: physical harm to things | harm: injury or hurt
example: The storm caused serious damage to roads. | There's no harm in asking.
typical_mistake: The flood caused many damages.
correction: The flood caused a lot of damage.
memory_tip: Damage is mostly for things (buildings, roads); harm is mostly for people and health (there's no harm in…).

definitions: almost: nearly | most: the majority of
example: Almost all students passed. | Most students passed.
typical_mistake: Almost students like music.
correction: Most students like music. / Almost all students like music.
mistake_note: almost can't go directly before a noun.
memory_tip: Almost = nearly, goes with all/every/no/always; most + noun = the majority (most students).

definitions: percent: out of a hundred (with a number) | percentage: a proportion, without a number
example: Sales rose by 20 percent. | The percentage of women in work increased.
typical_mistake: The percent of students who passed rose.
correction: The percentage of students who passed rose.
memory_tip: With a number → percent (20 percent); without a number → percentage (a high percentage of…).

definitions: person: one human | people: more than one person
example: Only one person was late. | Many people are waiting.
typical_mistake: There are many peoples in the room.
correction: There are many people in the room.
memory_tip: Person = one; people = more than one and already plural (people are). Peoples means 'nations'.

definitions: nature: the natural world | the environment: the natural world around us
example: We should protect nature. | Plastic harms the environment.
typical_mistake: We must protect the nature.
correction: We must protect nature.
memory_tip: Nature (the natural world) takes no the; the environment always takes the.
